newsitem.title: THAILAND: YEAREND-Thai baht seen facing weak market sentiment in 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Thai baht seen facing weak market sentiment in 1997.

text.p: The Thai baht weathered several market attacks in 1996 and will remain shaky next year under the weight of Thailand's sluggish economy and prolonged bearish stock market, analysts said.

"Baht sentiment will remain weak next year. Confidence will recover if the new government can convince people that the economy is not as bad as many think, and the stock market decline has bottomed out," Satian Tantanasarit, vice president of Thai Danu Bank Plc, told Reuters.
Thailand's sharply slowing economy and zero-growth exports have prompted a market flight out of the baht, which this year was occasionally the target of devaluation rumours.
The Thai economy is projected to grow less than seven percent in 1996, its slowest pace in a decade, while exports are expected to register zero growth.
A heavy baht sell-off in August prompted the Bank of Thailand to take an unprecedented step to defend the currency by intervening in both swap and spot markets in Singapore and Hong Kong.
In late December, the central bank was again forced to step in to slow the baht slide as year-end market demand for the dollar rose.
"(BOT's) recent intervention indirectly told the market that the baht fixing will be there in the near future," Singapore- based economist Jimmy Koh of I.D.A.E Inc said.
Thailand fixes the baht against a basket of currencies. The central bank does not disclose the basket content but the dollar is believed to carry the biggest weight, followed by the yen and the mark.

The central bank announces a daily baht/dollar mid-rate and it tries to stabilise the baht by agreeing to trade baht/dollar with commercial banks within a narrow two-satang range on either side of the mid-rate.
Analysts said the central bank's rigid foreign exchange system early this year induced a heavy influx of short-term foreign funds, brought in by speculators to arbitrage on high Thai interest rates.
The analysts expected the Bank of Thailand to try to improve its domestic money supply management by relaxing the rigid baht fixing but they did not know when the bank would make the move.
Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said recently the baht fixing practice should be flexible in the future but stressed that any change must not be at the expense of the currency's stability.
He said Thailand should stop relying on domestic interest rates as the sole mechanism for managing the baht, foreign capital flows and money supply.

"I think we should not be apprehensive about widening the baht band... provided any move affecting baht should not be made at the expense of its stability and strength. We could make (baht fixing) flexible but there must be stability, not volatility," he said.
Analysts said any fixing adjustment was unlikely to be made in the near term until Thai economic fundamentals improve.
"If the economy picks up, we might see the (baht band) widening prospect," said Singapore-based economist Ali Seng of MMS International.
